knowledge-base.overview: Language-specific idioms, guardrails, and patterns for Rust 2021 edition+. Loaded automatically when agents work on .rs files or Cargo.toml. Covers ownership, error handling with Result/Option, async with tokio, unsafe policy, testing, and tooling for systems programming, CLIs, APIs, and WebAssembly.

core-principles.principle: Every value has exactly one owner; borrowing is explicit. Design types so ownership is obvious at the call site.
Return Result<T, E> for all fallible operations. panic! signals a bug in the program, not a recoverable condition.
Iterators, generics, and traits compile away their overhead. Prefer them over manual loops and dynamic dispatch when performance is equal.
Default to #[forbid(unsafe_code)] at the crate root. Every unsafe block requires a written justification comment explaining the invariants upheld.
All code must pass cargo clippy -- -D warnings with zero suppressions. Suppressing a lint requires a comment explaining the exception.

guardrail.rule: unwrap() is forbidden outside test and example code. In production code use ? for propagation, or match/if let with a meaningful error path.
Never use String as an error type. Define a crate-level error enum with thiserror for library code, or use anyhow::Error for application (binary) code.
Every unsafe block must be preceded by a // SAFETY: comment explaining which invariants are upheld and why the operation is sound.
Run cargo fmt and cargo clippy -- -D warnings before every commit. Zero lint warnings are permitted in merged code.
All async operations must have timeouts. Use tokio::time::timeout to wrap any await that could block indefinitely.
guardrail.bad: let resp = client.get(url).send().await?; // hangs forever on network failure

guardrail.rule: Use expect("reason") only when the invariant is guaranteed by construction, and always include a comment explaining that invariant. Never use expect without a meaningful message.
guardrail.good: // The "version" key is inserted during Config::new() and never removed. let version = config.get("version").expect("version key always present after Config::new");

guardrail.rule: Use tokio::sync::Mutex (not std::sync::Mutex) in async contexts. Use Arc<T> for shared ownership across threads. Never use Rc<T> in async code.
guardrail.bad: let state = Arc::new(std::sync::Mutex::new(data)); // can deadlock in async

guardrail.rule: Prefer channels (mpsc, oneshot, broadcast) over shared mutable state for communication between tasks. Every select! branch must handle cancellation.
Use edition = "2021" in Cargo.toml. Set rust-version (MSRV) in Cargo.toml for all published crates. Use stable toolchain unless a nightly feature is explicitly justified.
guardrail.bad: [package] name = "mylib" version = "0.1.0" # no edition, no rust-version

guardrail.rule: Add #[must_use] to functions returning Result, Option, or any value whose discard is likely a bug.
guardrail.bad: pub fn save(&self) -> Result<(), StorageError> { ... } // caller can silently discard the Result

guardrail.rule: Commit Cargo.lock for binaries. Omit Cargo.lock from version control for libraries (add to .gitignore). Run cargo update weekly for security patches.
guardrail.bad: # .gitignore for a binary crate Cargo.lock # wrong — should be committed for binaries
guardrail.good: # Cargo.lock committed for binary crates # Cargo.lock in .gitignore for library crates

guardrail.rule: No global mutable state. Use dependency injection via function arguments or structs. If a lazy static is truly needed, use once_cell::sync::Lazy or std::sync::OnceLock.
guardrail.bad: static mut DB_POOL: Option<Pool> = None; // unsafe global mutable state

guardrail.rule: Prefer exhaustive match over if let chains when all variants matter. Use if let only for single-variant extraction where other variants are genuinely irrelevant.

Naming conventions: snake_case for functions/variables/modules/crate names; PascalCase for types/traits/enums/type parameters; SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for constants and statics. Derive order: Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash, Serialize, Deserialize.
guardrail.bad: fn GetUser() {} // should be get_user struct user_profile {} // should be UserProfile const maxRetries = 3; // should be MAX_RETRIES

pattern.name: Library Error Type (thiserror)
pattern.context: Any library crate that surfaces errors to callers
pattern.description: Define a crate-level error enum. Use #[from] for transparent wrapping of external errors. This gives callers typed, matchable errors.

pattern.name: Application Error Handling (anyhow)
pattern.context: Binary / application code where error details are for the operator
pattern.description: Use anyhow::Result and .context() / .with_context() to attach human-readable context at each call site. Use bail! for early-exit conditions.

pattern.name: ? Operator with From Conversions
pattern.context: Functions that call into multiple error domains
pattern.description: Define From impls via thiserror's #[from] attribute. The ? operator then converts automatically — no manual match on Result.

pattern.name: Async Handler with State Injection (axum)
pattern.description: Pass shared state via axum::extract::State. Keep handlers thin; delegate to service layer. Return typed responses.

pattern.name: Newtype Pattern
pattern.context: Domain primitives that must not be confused with raw types
pattern.description: Wrap primitives in single-field tuple structs to create distinct types the compiler can distinguish. Derive common traits for ergonomics.

pattern.name: Builder Pattern for Complex Structs
pattern.context: Types with many optional configuration fields
pattern.description: Use the typed builder pattern (or the bon / typed-builder crate) to avoid large argument lists and make optional fields explicit at the call site.
